Area.evidence_source: [page/4/Text/10] Participants referenced a range of perceptions that contributed to their low self-esteem, levels of personal stress, and, ultimately, their increased risk for suicide (see Figure 2). The first perception was their understandings of what it was to be a successful man, which involved, among others, the following limiting constructs: that successful or "real" men have high-powered (meaningful) jobs, lots of money, access to girls, are certainly not gay, are emotionally tough, do not need help, do not admit intrapersonal difficulties, and certainly do not admit to psychological problems: [page/6/Text/3] Participants referred to a wide variety of problems, each of which, to a greater or lesser extent, elevated their risk of suicide. Such problems included physically, emotionally, and sexually dysfunctional or abusive childhoods and family backgrounds; poor or low self-image; relationship difficulties and breakdowns; drug abuse and addiction; and general and specific anxieties. [page/5/Text/9] Participants stressed the therapeutic value of being able to mix with people who had survived similar circumstances; this helped them to appreciate they were "not the only ones like this." Moreover, they were able to verbalize how they were feeling in a forum in which they were not afraid of being labeled as crazy or weird. Such contact and interaction served to normalize suicide, normalize their difficulties and, ultimately, normalize them as human beings: [page/6/Text/1] Finally, hearing these testimonies served as a protective factor against future suicide attempts. [page/6/Text/3] In some cases, the young men had been able to access counseling therapy (e.g., cognitive behavioral therapy [CBT]) within mental health services.
